title: About The Green Yard
text:
Planting a Sweet Granadilla




My name is Schuyler Hamilton and I am a native Arizonan. I absolutely love Phoenix and after living in mutiple states around the country during College I decided to come back to my home. Growing up my mom used to garden, we would grow all kinds of vegetables and they also had several mature citrus trees (Navel Orange, Grapefruit and Mandarin) in their Green Yard. This exposed me to the world of growing your own food. During High School and College I got away from gardening and focusing on other aspects of life including Photography and Videography. My oldest son was born in 2018 and my life was never the same again. Not only did he change every aspect of living but I also awakened my passion for growing my own food. In early spring of 2019 I bought my first Banana plants (Blue Java and Dwarf Nam Wah) and planted them in our old Green Yard.

Implemented new strategies that increased efficiency by 30%.
Led a team of 10 professionals in achieving project milestones.




Office Team







Studied Computer Science with a focus on artificial intelligence and machine learning.

title: Inside a High-Density Florida Food Forest Packed with Tropical Diversity
text:
KC has transformed approximately 0.17 acres into a densely planted Florida
    food forest filled with tropical fruit trees, edible plants, and unusual
    species. This tour shows how tremendous diversity can be grown on a small
    residential property when every layer of the landscape is used thoughtfully.
  

  
    
    
  

  

    
      Location
      Florida
    

    
      Host
      KC
    

    
      Property Size
      Approximately 0.17 Acres
    

    
      Garden Type
      Residential Food Forest
    

    
      Growing Style
      High-Density, Multilayered
    

    
      Primary Focus
      Tropical Fruit Diversity
    

  


  

    About This Florida Food Forest

    
      A food forest does not need to occupy several acres to contain remarkable
      diversity. KC’s garden demonstrates how a relatively small residential
      property can become a densely layered edible landscape.
    

    
      Rather than treating each fruit tree as an isolated specimen surrounded
      by open space, the garden uses close planting, vertical layers, and nearly
      every available growing area. The result is a living collection in which
      tropical fruit trees, shrubs, vines, and smaller edible plants grow
      together throughout the property.
    

    
      During this tour, we explore the plants, layout, and growing decisions
      that allow KC to maintain such an extensive collection in a limited area.
      The garden offers ideas for anyone interested in increasing diversity
      without owning a large farm or homestead.
    

  


  

    What You’ll Learn

    

      
        How a small residential property can hold an extensive edible collection
      

      
        How high-density planting differs from a conventional orchard layout
      

      
        How multiple vertical layers make better use of limited garden space
      

      
        Why plant placement becomes especially important in a crowded food forest
      

      
        How tropical fruit diversity can become the central theme of a home landscape
      

      
        Ideas that can be adapted to smaller backyards and urban properties
      

    

  


  

    What Makes This Garden Abundant?

    
      The defining feature of this food forest is its density. Instead of
      relying on a few large trees separated by open lawn, the garden fits many
      edible species into a compact residential landscape.
    

    
      The abundance comes not only from the number of plants, but from the way
      the available space is used. Taller trees create an upper layer, smaller
      fruit trees and shrubs occupy the middle, while vines, herbs, and other
      edible plants fill additional niches.
    

    
      KC’s garden shows that abundance can mean diversity, experimentation, and
      the ability to step outside and encounter something edible almost
      everywhere you look.
    

  


  

    Shorts From This Tour

    
      These five short videos will highlight individual plants, lessons, and
      memorable moments from the full tour. We can replace each placeholder
      once the Shorts are published.
    

    

      
        Short 1
        
          Featured Plant
          
            A closer look at one of the standout tropical plants growing in the garden.
          
        
      

      
        Short 2
        
          High-Density Design
          
            See how KC fits an impressive number of edible species into a small space.
          
        
      

      
        Short 3
        
          Rare Tropical Fruit
          
            Discover one of the unusual fruit species featured during the tour.
          
        
      

      
        Short 4
        
          Planting in Layers
          
            A quick example of how vertical layers increase the garden’s diversity.
          
        
      

      
        Short 5
        
          KC’s Growing Lesson
          
            One practical idea or lesson that other home growers can apply.
          
        
      

    

  


  

    Species Seen in This Tour

    
      This section will become the verified plant database for the property.
      We should add plants only after confirming that they appear in the tour.
    

    
      Verified species list coming soon
      Tropical fruit trees
      Smaller fruiting shrubs
      Edible vines
      Herbs and support plants
      Rare or unusual edible species
    

    
      As the species database grows, each plant name can link to its own profile
      showing every tour where that species appears, the climates where it is
      growing, and future nursery or resource links.
    

  


  

    Key Ideas From the Tour

    
      
        A small residential property can support far more edible diversity than
        a conventional yard.
      
      
        Vertical layering helps growers make better use of limited land.
      
      
        Dense planting requires thoughtful placement and ongoing observation.
      
      
        A food forest can function as both a productive landscape and a living
        collection of unusual plants.
      
      
        Abundance does not always mean owning more land—it can mean using the
        space you already have more creatively.

title: This Florida Food Forest Is Packed with Tropical Diversity
text:
The Story
A food forest does not need to occupy several acres to contain remarkable diversity.
In this Florida garden, KC has used approximately 0.17 acres to grow an extensive collection of tropical fruit trees and edible plants. The tour offers a close look at how plants can be layered, grouped, and fitted into a residential landscape without treating each tree as an isolated specimen.
This section can later become the complete written story of the garden, including how KC began growing, how the property developed, the biggest challenges, and the ideas visitors can apply in their own yards.

title: This Florida Food Forest Is Packed with Tropical Diversity
text:
What Makes This Garden Abundant?
The defining feature of this food forest is its density.
Rather than leaving large open spaces between individual trees, the garden uses vertical layers and close planting to create room for a much wider range of edible species. That approach allows a small property to function as an unusually diverse living collection.

title: This Florida Food Forest Is Packed with Tropical Diversity
text:
Growing Lessons From This Tour

Small properties can hold considerable diversity.
Vertical layers help make better use of limited growing space.
Dense planting can create a food-forest environment rather than a conventional orchard layout.
Plant selection and placement matter when many species share a small area.
A residential landscape can become both productive and highly diverse.
